title: Breakfast by the Sea and Peter Restored
summary: Back in Galilee, seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing until the risen Jesus, unrecognized on the shore, tells them where to cast the net. He feeds them breakfast by a charcoal fire, then asks Peter three times whether he loves him and three times commissions him to feed his sheep, foretelling the death by which Peter will glorify God. The Gospel ends by identifying the beloved disciple as its witness and author.
story:
John 20 closed with what reads like the end of the book (20:30-31). Chapter 21 is an epilogue that ties up threads left hanging. The first is Peter. He had boasted that he would lay down his life for Jesus and been told he would deny him three times before the rooster crowed (13:37-38); he did so beside a charcoal fire (18:18, 25-27), and although he has seen the risen Lord, nothing has yet been said about his failure. The second is the future: what will become of the disciples, and in particular of Peter and the beloved disciple, now that Jesus is going to the Father. Jesus had told Peter at the supper that he could not follow him now but would follow later (13:36), and here that word is explained.

The chapter returns to Galilee, where the signs began (2:11), to the lake where Jesus fed the five thousand (6:1), to ordinary work and an ordinary meal. There Jesus reveals himself a third time to the disciples (verse 14), restores a failed disciple, sends him out as a shepherd, and tells him how his road will end. The last verses name the witness behind the whole Gospel and close with a confession that the world itself could not hold all that Jesus did.
historical:
The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about 21 kilometers (13 miles) long and 13 kilometers (8 miles) wide, lying some 210 meters below sea level in the rift valley of the Jordan. It took this name from the city of Tiberias, which Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee, founded on its western shore about AD 20 in honor of the emperor Tiberius; Josephus says it was built over tombs, so that observant Jews were reluctant to settle there (Antiquities 18.36-38). John alone among the Gospels uses the name (6:1, 6:23, 21:1), perhaps because it was the name his later readers knew.

Fishing was a major industry around the lake. Magdala, the hometown of Mary Magdalene, is commonly identified with the town Josephus calls Taricheae, a Greek name that refers to salting fish. In 1986, during a drought, two fishermen from Kibbutz Ginosar found the remains of a wooden boat in the mud of the northwestern shore. The Galilee boat is about 8.2 meters (27 feet) long and 2.3 meters (7.5 feet) wide and has been dated between about 100 BC and AD 70; a boat of this size could have carried a crew like the seven disciples of verse 2. Mendel Nun, a fisherman of Kibbutz Ein Gev who studied the lake's fishing for decades (The Sea of Galilee and Its Fishermen in the New Testament, 1989), described how nets were cast at night near the shore, and how someone standing on land can sometimes see a shoal that those in the boat cannot.

Verses 18 and 19 point to Peter's martyrdom. The letter known as 1 Clement, written from Rome about AD 96, speaks of Peter's witness and death (1 Clement 5). Tacitus describes Nero's persecution of Christians in Rome after the great fire of AD 64, some of them crucified (Annals 15.44). Tertullian, early in the third century, read Jesus' words about another girding Peter as fulfilled when Peter was bound to the cross (Scorpiace 15), and Eusebius reports, citing Origen, that Peter asked to be crucified head downward (Church History 3.1). The presbyter Gaius, about AD 200, spoke of the trophies, or memorials, of Peter and Paul on the Vatican hill and the road to Ostia (Church History 2.25), and excavations under St Peter's Basilica from 1940 to 1949 uncovered a small second-century shrine that many identify with the one Gaius knew.

The rumor that the beloved disciple would not die (verse 23) suggests he lived to a great age and that his death, or approaching death, needed explaining. Irenaeus, writing about AD 180, says that John the disciple of the Lord, who leaned on his breast, lived at Ephesus into the reign of Trajan, who became emperor in AD 98 (Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1, 3.3.4). Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus about AD 190, says that John who leaned on the Lord's breast was buried there (Eusebius, Church History 5.24.3). Papias, an early second-century bishop, mentions both the apostle John and a John the Elder (Church History 3.39.4), which has led some scholars to distinguish the beloved disciple from the son of Zebedee.
cultural:
Night was the best time for fishing with nets on the lake, when fish came nearer the surface and the shore and the nets were harder for them to see; a fruitless night was a familiar frustration (compare Luke 5:5). Jesus' call, “Children, do you have any fish?” (verse 5), uses paidia, an affectionate address (1 John 2:18 uses the same word), and asks about prosphagion, something to eat with bread, which on the lake meant fish. Peter, who had stripped for work (the Greek gumnos, naked, often meant lightly clad, wearing only an undergarment), tucks his outer garment around himself before jumping in, an odd but natural detail: a Jew would not greet anyone, least of all his Lord, undressed. A hundred yards is literally two hundred cubits, a cubit being the length of a forearm, about 45 centimeters, so about 90 meters.

The charcoal fire (anthrakia) deliberately recalls the fire in the high priest's courtyard; the Greek word occurs only in these two places in the New Testament. Fish (opsarion, cooked fish, the same word used at the feeding in 6:9 and 6:11) and bread were the ordinary food of Galilee. Sharing a meal was an act of fellowship and acceptance in the ancient world, and a host who served his guests with his own hands honored them; Jesus, who washed the disciples' feet (13:1-15), now cooks for them. Counting the catch was practical, since the proceeds were shared among partners, and the number 153 has the look of a remembered tally.

Shepherding was the Old Testament's great image for leadership. God is Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23, Psalm 80:1), and kings and priests were meant to be shepherds under him. Ezekiel condemns the shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock and promises that God himself will shepherd his sheep and set over them one shepherd, his servant David (Ezekiel 34:1-24; compare Jeremiah 23:1-4). When Jesus, the good shepherd of chapter 10, tells Peter to feed and shepherd his sheep, he entrusts him with the care Jesus himself has shown, and the sheep remain his: my lambs, my sheep. Girding, tying up the long garment with a belt, was what one did before work or walking (Exodus 12:11, Luke 12:35); to be girded by another and led where one does not wish was the condition of a prisoner.
literary:
The chapter has two halves, a scene of recognition and provision (verses 1 to 14) and a dialogue of restoration and calling (verses 15 to 23), followed by a closing testimony (verses 24 and 25). It is framed by the verb phaneroō, to reveal or manifest: Jesus revealed himself (verse 1, twice) and this was the third time he appeared (verse 14), counting the appearances to the disciples in 20:19 and 20:26. The catch of fish closely resembles the call of the first disciples in Luke 5:1-11, where Peter also fishes all night without success, lets down the nets at Jesus' word, and responds to the catch with a sudden move toward Jesus; the meal of bread and fish by the lake echoes the feeding of the five thousand (John 6:1-13), where Jesus also took bread and gave it.

The dialogue is built on threes: three questions, three answers, three commands, answering Peter's three denials, and Peter is grieved precisely because Jesus asked a third time (verse 17). Jesus addresses him as Simon son of John, the name by which he first met him (1:42), not as Peter, the Rock. The prophecy of Peter's death is introduced with the same phrase used of Jesus' own death, signifying by what kind of death (12:33, 18:32, 21:19), and ends with Follow Me, the Gospel's first call to discipleship (1:43) now given with the cost made plain. Peter and the beloved disciple are paired here as throughout the second half of the Gospel (13:23-24, 18:15-16, 20:2-10): the beloved disciple recognizes the Lord first (verse 7), Peter acts first; one is called to follow to martyrdom, the other to remain and bear witness.

The number 153 has attracted many symbolic readings. Augustine observed that it is the sum of the numbers from 1 to 17 and read 17 as the ten commandments and the sevenfold Spirit (Tractates on John 122). Jerome claimed that Greek naturalists counted 153 kinds of fish, citing the poet Oppian, but Oppian's surviving work does not say so, and Robert Grant showed that the claim cannot be confirmed. J. A. Emerton (Journal of Theological Studies, 1958) noted that the Hebrew letters of En-gedi and En-eglaim, the two places where fishermen spread their nets in Ezekiel's vision of the river from the temple (Ezekiel 47:10), have numerical values of 17 and 153, and Richard Bauckham has developed that proposal. John gives no hint of symbolism, and it may simply be the remembered count of astonished fishermen. The unbroken net (verse 11) uses the verb schizō, from which schism comes, and some readers see a picture of the church's unity, as with the untorn tunic (19:24).

The Gospel's two endings match each other. Bauckham (The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple, 2007) observed that 20:30-31 and 21:24-25 each contain 43 Greek words, and that the prologue has 496 syllables and the epilogue 496 words; whether such counts reflect the author's design is disputed. The book's last sentence, with its world too small for the books, is a deliberate overstatement of wonder, and it is the only place in the Gospel where the narrator says I.

outline.t: Seven disciples go fishing and catch nothing
Jesus on the shore and the great catch
Do you love Me? Peter restored and commissioned
The witness and the many untold things

doctrines.note: Jesus does not ignore Peter's denial or shame him for it. He reopens the wound gently, by another charcoal fire, with three questions matching three failures, and brings Peter to confess his love, not his own strength: “Lord, You know all things” (verse 17). Restoration in this chapter comes through honest facing of failure in the presence of mercy, and it ends not in private relief but in renewed calling.

The risen Jesus entrusts his flock to a human shepherd. Peter's commission to feed and shepherd the sheep shows that the church's leaders serve people who belong to Christ (my lambs, my sheep), not to themselves, and that love for Christ is the qualification for the task. Peter later urges elders to “Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you” (1 Peter 5:2), and churches differ over how far this charge is unique to Peter and how far it belongs to every pastor.

Jesus' question is not whether Peter is sorry, competent, or brave, but whether he loves him. Love for Christ is the root of service and is shown in care for his people: the answer to each confession of love is a command to feed his sheep. The chapter joins the two great commands, love for God and love for neighbor, in a single conversation.

“If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?” (verse 22). Jesus speaks of his coming again as certain while refusing to set its time, and the narrator corrects a rumor built on his words (verse 23). The chapter holds together a sure hope of Christ's return and a refusal to use it for speculation about particular people or dates.

Jesus tells Peter by what death he will glorify God and refuses to satisfy his curiosity about the beloved disciple. Each disciple has his own calling and end under the Lord's hand, and even a martyr's death is described as glorifying God. The command is the same for both: Follow Me.

words.note: Phaneroō, to reveal, make visible, manifest. It occurs about 49 times in the New Testament and 9 times in John, three of them in this chapter (twice in verse 1 and in verse 14). John uses it for Jesus' glory revealed at Cana (2:11), for the works of God displayed in the man born blind (9:3), and for the Father's name made known (17:6). Here the risen Jesus reveals himself, and the verb frames the fishing scene as another sign in which the disciples come to know who he is.

Anthrakia, a charcoal fire, a heap of glowing coals. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, in 18:18, where Peter warms himself and denies Jesus, and in verse 9 here, where Jesus has breakfast ready. The rarity of the word makes the link unmistakable: the place of Peter's failure is recreated as the place of his restoration.

Agapaō, to love, occurs about 143 times in the New Testament and 37 times in John. Jesus uses it in his first two questions (verses 15 and 16), and it describes the disciple whom Jesus loved (verses 7 and 20). Peter answers each time with phileō, and in the third question Jesus uses phileō. B. F. Westcott (1881) and many preachers since have seen a deliberate contrast between self-giving love and lesser affection. D. A. Carson and many others note that John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere (the Father loves the Son with agapaō in 3:35 and phileō in 5:20), that Peter's grief is tied to the question being asked a third time, not to a change of verb, and that John varies his vocabulary throughout the passage (lambs and sheep, feed and shepherd, know and know). Most modern commentators read the change as stylistic variation.

Phileō, to love, have affection for, and sometimes to kiss. It occurs about 25 times in the New Testament and 13 times in John, where it is used of the Father's love for the Son (5:20), of Jesus' love for Lazarus (11:3, 11:36), and of the Father's love for the disciples (16:27). Peter uses it in all three answers. The word is related to philos, friend, the word Jesus used when he said he no longer called the disciples servants but friends (15:14-15).

Boskō, to feed, tend, graze, occurs 9 times in the New Testament, mostly of herdsmen feeding pigs (Mark 5:11, 5:14, Luke 15:15) and in John only in verses 15 and 17. It emphasizes nourishing the flock. Jesus' three commands alternate: feed my lambs (verse 15), shepherd my sheep (verse 16), feed my sheep (verse 17), and together they describe the whole care of the flock, from the youngest to the grown.

Poimainō, to shepherd, occurs 11 times in the New Testament. It includes feeding but also guiding, protecting, and ruling, and in Revelation it is used for ruling the nations (Revelation 2:27, 19:15) as well as for the Lamb who will shepherd his people to springs of living water (Revelation 7:17). Paul uses it for the elders of Ephesus shepherding the church of God (Acts 20:28), and 1 Peter 5:2 urges elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, perhaps remembering this morning.

Akoloutheō, to follow, go after, be a disciple. It occurs about 90 times in the New Testament and 19 times in John. It can describe simply walking behind someone, as the beloved disciple does in verse 20, and it is the Gospels' word for discipleship. Jesus' first words to Philip were “Follow Me” (1:43); he told Peter at the supper that he could not follow him now but would follow later (13:36); and here, after foretelling Peter's death, he says it again (verses 19 and 22). Following now includes following to a cross.

Menō, to remain, stay, abide, continue, occurs about 118 times in the New Testament and some 40 times in John, more than in any other book, where it describes abiding in Jesus and his word (8:31, 15:4-10). In verses 22 and 23 it is used in its plain sense of remaining alive, if I want him to remain until I return. The misunderstanding of that word produced a rumor the narrator corrects, and the verb's deeper Johannine sense suggests that the beloved disciple's calling was to remain as a witness while Peter's was to follow to martyrdom.

christ:
The risen Christ in this chapter is the same Lord who called fishermen, fed the hungry, and washed feet. He comes to his disciples in the middle of their frustration, a fruitless night, and provides abundantly, and he is already cooking when they land: he invites them to bring some of what they caught, but the meal is his. He knows all things, as Peter says, including the depths of Peter's love and weakness, and still entrusts him with his flock. In doing so he acts as the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11) and as the one shepherd God promised to set over his people (Ezekiel 34:23), and he makes Peter a shepherd under him, not in his place.

He is Lord of the future as well. He can say how Peter will glorify God in death, echoing his own glorification on the cross, and whether the beloved disciple will remain until he comes. The phrase until I return is a clear statement of the hope of Christ's coming again. His final call, Follow Me, is the same word with which the Gospels begin the life of discipleship, now spoken to a man who knows what it will cost.

The chapter ends by grounding the whole Gospel in testimony. The disciple whom Jesus loved has borne witness and written, and his witness is true (verse 24). Christ is known through the testimony of those who saw him, and the Gospel's closing words confess that no book, not even all the books the world could hold, can contain him.
interpretation:
The fathers read this chapter as the church in miniature. Augustine (Tractates on John 122) saw in the 153 fish the whole company of the saved, drawn by the law and the Spirit, and in the unbroken net the church at the end of the age; he read the threefold question as love answering threefold denial (Tractate 123), and he read Peter and John as figures of two lives, Peter of the active life of labor and suffering that follows Christ now, John of the contemplative life that will be completed only when Christ comes (Tractate 124). In the same tractate he reports, without endorsing it, a legend that John was lying asleep in his tomb at Ephesus and that the earth over it stirred with his breathing. Tertullian cited verse 18 as a prophecy of Peter's crucifixion (Scorpiace 15), and Origen, as Eusebius reports, added that Peter was crucified head downward (Church History 3.1).

The commissioning of Peter became a central text in debates over authority in the church. The First Vatican Council's constitution Pastor Aeternus (1870, chapter 1) cited verses 15 to 17, with Matthew 16:18-19, as the moment when Christ gave Peter alone jurisdiction as supreme shepherd over the whole flock. Orthodox interpreters have generally read the scene as Peter's restoration to the apostolic office he shared with the others, and Protestant interpreters, following Calvin's commentary (1553), as a personal restoration and a charge that applies to every faithful pastor, as 1 Peter 5:1-4 applies it to the elders. The apocryphal Acts of Peter (late second century) tells the story of Peter fleeing Rome and meeting Jesus, who says he is going to be crucified again, which sends Peter back to his death; Henryk Sienkiewicz's novel Quo Vadis (1896) made the legend famous.

In art, Konrad Witz's The Miraculous Draught of Fishes (1444, Geneva) sets this scene on Lake Geneva with Peter wading toward the shore, and is often called the first European painting to portray a real, recognizable stretch of countryside. Raphael's cartoon Christ's Charge to Peter (1515 to 1516, now in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London) was designed for tapestries in the Sistine Chapel, and Caravaggio's Crucifixion of Saint Peter (1601, Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome) shows the apostle being raised head downward. At Tabgha on the lake's northwest shore the Franciscan Church of the Primacy of Saint Peter, built in 1933 on older foundations, encloses a rock venerated as the table where Jesus served breakfast. In the Revised Common Lectionary verses 1 to 19 are read on the Third Sunday of Easter in Year C.

Modern critical study has concentrated on the chapter's origin (see below). Rudolf Bultmann (1941), Raymond Brown (1966 to 1970), and C. K. Barrett (1955) regarded it as an appendix added by a later editor or by the evangelist's circle; Paul Minear (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1983) and Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006; The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple, 2007) argued that it belongs to the Gospel's design as an intended epilogue.
text:
Every surviving manuscript of John that preserves the end of the Gospel contains chapter 21. A small third-century papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, P109, preserves parts of verses 18 to 20 and 23 to 25. The fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus has an intriguing feature: when H. J. M. Milne and T. C. Skeat examined it under ultraviolet light in the 1930s, they found that the scribe first ended the Gospel at verse 24, drew the decorative end mark and wrote the closing title, then washed them out and added verse 25. The scribe's exemplar may have lacked the last verse, or he may simply have corrected his own omission; either way, verse 25 is present in the finished codex. Tertullian once called 20:31 the close of the Gospel (Against Praxeas 25), yet he knew and cited 21:18 (Scorpiace 15). In some medieval manuscripts, the family of minuscules led by minuscules 1 and 1582, the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11) is placed after 21:25 with a note that it was moved there from chapter 8.

Other differences affect English Bibles. In verses 15 to 17 the King James Version reads ‘Simon, son of Jonas’, following later manuscripts that assimilated the name to Matthew 16:17; the earliest manuscripts read Simon son of John, as in 1:42. The King James Version ends verse 25 with ‘Amen’, which is absent from the earliest witnesses.

Several differences are matters of translation. In verse 5 Jesus' address paidia is ‘Children’ (KJV, ESV, BSB) or ‘Friends’ (NIV). In verse 7 the KJV says Peter was ‘naked’, the ESV that he ‘was stripped for work’, and the BSB that he had removed his outer garment. In verse 15 more than these is ambiguous in Greek and English alike: it may mean more than these other disciples love me, more than you love these disciples, or more than you love these things, the boat, the nets, and the fishing; most commentators favor the first, recalling Peter's earlier claim to a loyalty greater than the others' (Mark 14:29). English cannot show the alternation between agapaō and phileō in verses 15 to 17, and some versions mark it in a note.

teach.big: The risen Jesus meets his failed disciples in their ordinary work, feeds them, restores Peter through love rather than shame, and calls each disciple to follow him in his own appointed way, whatever it costs.

outline.t: After Easter the disciples return to familiar work, and without Jesus their best effort brings nothing.
Jesus' word turns failure into abundance; love recognizes him first, and Peter cannot wait to reach him.
The risen Lord serves breakfast: before he asks anything of his disciples, he feeds them.
Jesus restores Peter by asking about love, three times for three denials, and gives him work to do for the flock that remains Christ's own.
Following Jesus includes a cross: Peter will glorify God by his death, and the call is simply Follow Me.
Comparison with other disciples is a distraction; each is responsible for his own obedience, and Jesus' words must not be twisted into rumor.
The Gospel rests on true testimony, and Jesus is greater than anything that can be written about him.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The most common is to build a sermon on the difference between agapaō and phileō, as though Jesus asked for divine love and Peter could offer only friendship. The case for a strong distinction is weak: John uses the verbs interchangeably elsewhere, and the text says Peter was hurt because he was asked a third time. The point is the threefold restoration, not a lexical ladder.

A second misreading allegorizes the 153 fish into a code and builds doctrine on it; the proposals are interesting, but none is certain, and John does not explain the number. A third treats the scene as a polemic for or against papal primacy and nothing else. Teachers can acknowledge that Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions read the commission differently while keeping the text's plain force: a failed disciple is forgiven and given care of Christ's people. A fourth turns Peter's restoration into a lesson that failure does not matter. Jesus does not pretend the denial never happened; he brings Peter back to the fire. A fifth uses verse 22 to speculate about the timing of Christ's return, the very misuse verse 23 corrects.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on anyone living with a failure they cannot undo: a betrayal, a public fall, a broken promise to God. Peter's restoration shows that Jesus neither ignores such failure nor defines a person by it. Teach it with care for those who have been harmed by leaders who fell; restoration to fellowship is not the same as a quick return to authority, and the text's emphasis on love and care for the flock guards against using it to excuse abuse. It also speaks to people facing suffering or death, who may take comfort that even Peter's death was known to Jesus and could glorify God, and to those who compare their lot with others'.

hard.q: Was chapter 21 part of the original Gospel, or was it added later by someone else?
hard.a:
The case for a later addition is strong and widely held. The Gospel seems to end at 20:30-31, which sums up the purpose of the book as a conclusion would; chapter 21 then begins again with After these things. Verse 24 speaks of the beloved disciple in the third person and adds we know that his testimony is true, which sounds like a group vouching for a witness who is not the writer of that sentence. Verse 23 corrects a rumor that he would not die, which many read as a response to his death. Some scholars have also argued that the vocabulary and style differ from chapters 1 to 20. On these grounds Rudolf Bultmann (commentary, 1941) assigned the chapter to an ecclesiastical editor, and Raymond Brown (Anchor Bible, 1966 to 1970), C. K. Barrett (1955), and Rudolf Schnackenburg regarded it as an appendix from the evangelist's circle, added when the Gospel was published in its final form. Critics who doubt the Gospel's eyewitness basis go further and take the we of verse 24 as evidence that the book was produced by later followers who attributed it to a revered figure.

Others argue that the chapter was always intended. No manuscript of John lacks it, and the Gospel apparently never circulated without it. Paul Minear (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1983) argued that the chapter completes themes the Gospel had left open, above all Peter's denial and the prediction that Peter would follow later (13:36), and that 20:30-31 concludes only the signs, not the whole book. Richard Bauckham (The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple, 2007) has argued that 21 is a planned epilogue balancing the prologue, pointing to matching word counts in the two endings and to the Greek convention of an author speaking of himself in the third person. Many who think the chapter was added later still hold that it comes from the same author, or from those who worked with him and preserved his testimony, rather than from a stranger; the style of the chapter, on their reading, is recognizably Johannine.

The question is literary and historical, not a question of the chapter's authority. Every Christian tradition has received John 21 as Scripture, and its canonical status has never been in doubt. Readers can weigh the arguments on its origin while reading it as the Gospel's own final word.

hard.q: Who is the beloved disciple who wrote this Gospel, and can his testimony be trusted?
hard.a:
The Gospel never names him, and the question has been open since the nineteenth century. Skeptical scholars argue that the beloved disciple may be an idealized figure or a symbol of the Johannine community rather than a real eyewitness, or that the Gospel's claim to eyewitness authority is a later device, like the attributions of other ancient writings to famous names. They note that John differs from the Synoptic Gospels in chronology, style, and the long discourses of Jesus, and argue that it reflects late first-century theology more than memory.

Church tradition from the late second century identifies the disciple with John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.1.1, about AD 180), who claimed a link to that generation through Polycarp, says that John the disciple of the Lord, who leaned on his breast, published the Gospel at Ephesus. This remains a widely held view; the sons of Zebedee are present in verse 2, and John son of Zebedee is otherwise curiously absent by name from this Gospel. Other scholars propose a disciple from Jerusalem who was not one of the Twelve, which would explain his acquaintance with the high priest (18:15-16). Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) identifies him with John the Elder known to Papias, and some have proposed Lazarus, the one of whom it is said that Jesus loved him (11:3, 11:5). Raymond Brown and others thought a circle of the disciple's followers shaped the final text, as the we of 21:24 may suggest.

On any of these views the Gospel presents itself as resting on eyewitness testimony (19:35, 21:24), and it is candid about the failures of its witnesses, including Peter's denial and Thomas's doubt. Bauckham has argued that ancient readers valued eyewitness testimony highly and that the Gospel's claim should be taken seriously as a historical claim. Readers will weigh that claim differently, but the Gospel asks to be read as testimony, not as legend.

observe: What were the disciples doing when Jesus appeared, and what happened when they followed his instruction?
What three questions does Jesus ask Peter, and what three commands does he give in reply?
What rumor spread about the beloved disciple, and how does the narrator correct it?
interpret: Jesus meets Peter by a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire where Peter denied him. Why might Jesus bring him back to that memory rather than avoid it?
What is the connection between loving Jesus and feeding his sheep? Why does Jesus answer each confession of love with a task?
What does Jesus mean by saying that Peter's death would glorify God, and how does that compare with what the Gospel says about Jesus' own death?
apply: Where do you need Jesus to bring you back to a place of failure, not to shame you but to restore you?
Peter's restoration comes with a responsibility for others. Whom has Christ given you to care for, and how are you feeding them?
Peter asked, What about him? Where does comparison with other believers distract you from following Jesus yourself?
